title: Karma starts with desire
hookLine: Yajnavalkya tells King Janaka where karma really starts: one step before the deed, in what you want
carry: karma starts with what you want
tomorrow: neti, neti — the great unborn self
last: DEATH IS A CROSSING, CARRYING WHAT WE DID.

cards: In January, the gym fills up: new shoes, new plans, a firm decision. By March, a lot of the new faces are gone. It usually isn't for lack of information; plenty of them knew what to do.
They made a resolution, and it didn't hold.
Yajnavalkya, still talking with King Janaka about what happens after death, stops to explain where a life actually comes from, and it's one step further back than the January crowd starts.

teach.h: AS ONE ACTS, SO ONE BECOMES.
teach.b: As a person acts, he says, as a person behaves, so they become. Doing good, one becomes good. Doing harm, one becomes harmful.
That's the karma Artabhaga heard about in private, now said out loud to a king. But then he goes deeper.

teach.h: A PERSON IS MADE OF DESIRE.
teach.b: Some say, he adds, a person is made of desire. And here's the line: yathakamo bhavati tat kratur bhavati. As is the desire, so is the will.
As is the will, so is the deed. As is the deed, so is what one becomes. Four steps.
Desire, the wanting underneath. Kratu, the will or resolve, the decision you make. The deed, the thing you actually do.

teach.h: DESIRE, WILL, DEED, WHAT YOU REACH.
teach.b: And what you reach, what you turn into.
The January crowd starts at step two, the resolution, and wonders why it doesn't hold.

teach.h: KARMA STARTS WITH WHAT YOU WANT.
teach.b: The text says the resolution grows out of what you actually want. That's a big turn in Hindu thought: karma isn't only what your hands do. It starts in the heart, with the wanting.
Then Yajnavalkya follows it past death. The one who still desires goes on, carried by the deed to what the mind clung to, and when that's spent, comes back to act again.
But the one who doesn't desire, whose only desire is the self, doesn't wander.
And then a verse the Katha Upanishad shares: when all the desires that live in the heart are let go, the mortal becomes immortal, and reaches Brahman, here. And the body?
It lies like a snake's old skin on an anthill, dead and cast off.

how: Hindu teachers cite this verse to explain karma as growing from desire and intention, not only from outward acts; the line about letting go of the heart's desires (4.4.7) also appears in the Katha Upanishad.

o: the deed itself, the thing you actually do
a desire buried deep in the heart
will, resolve: the step between wanting and doing

games.q: the four steps — tap the pairs.

s: the verse says the deed comes first and desire follows
desire first, then will, then deed, then what one becomes.
the one whose only desire is the self doesn't wander, the text says
being Brahman, he goes to Brahman.
the text compares the cast-off body to a snake's old skin
lying on an anthill, dead and cast off.

games.q: you've made a firm resolution three times and it never holds. according to this verse, where should you look?
o: at what you actually desire, underneath it.
games.why: as is the desire, so is the will. the resolution grows out of the wanting, so the text sends you one step further back.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you did today, small or large, and ask what you decided that made you do it. Then go one step further, to what you wanted underneath the decision. Don't judge the want; just find it, and let it be seen.

wordCard.voice: Kratu, will, resolve, purpose. The step between what you want and what you do: as the desire, so the kratu.

orig.note: Sanskrit kratu: will, resolve, purpose. yathākāmo bhavati tat kratur bhavati (4.4.5).

carryVoice: Your line: karma starts with what you want. As the desire, so the will, so the deed. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.6–7 (the one who does not desire; the snake's skin)
Katha Upanishad 2.3.14 (when all desires of the heart are let go)
